cita: Jonsater & Svensson (2026). Assessing Continuity in Agentic Development Across Multiple Development Cycles.
problema: Long-running coding agents working on the same codebase across multiple development cycles/sessions lose continuity of prior architectural and stylistic decisions because of limited context windows: each session is treated independently, so mid-session decisions from earlier cycles are forgotten unless explicitly re-supplied.
mecanismo: Empirically compares 5 combinations of 3 context-engineering strategies injected via an AGENTS.md file for the Codex CLI agent: (1) no strategy (baseline), (2) to-do list only (a JSON step/status/notes log the agent must consult before acting), (3) decision log only (a persistent JSON log of significant technical/architectural decisions the agent must consult before new work and update whenever a decision is made), (4) session summary only (an end-of-session JSON summary the agent reads at the start of the next session), (5) all three combined. Each combination runs 3 iterations across 2 development cycles on a mock web-dev project with predefined mid-session architectural decisions, scoring whether each decision persists into cycle 2.
evaluacion: Controlled mock web-development project (React/Vite/TypeScript) across 2 development cycles, 3 iterations per combination, with a human-scored decision-compliance rubric over 4 mid-session decisions, a requirement-compliance score, prompt/completion token consumption, generation time, and generation-error counts (Figures 4.1-4.9).
numeros_clave: Any persistent context-management strategy beats the no-strategy baseline on decision consistency. Combination 3 (decision log only) achieved the highest decision consistency while having the lowest generation time and cost among the tested strategies (section 5.2-5.3). Combination 5 (all 3 strategies, maximal context) showed declining requirement compliance, higher generation time/cost, and the most generation errors, attributed to 'context rot' from excess saved context. Decision 1 ('append "(Heading)"') success rate only 33.33% (achieved only in combinations 3-4) vs decision 2 (creation-timestamp comment) ranging 11.11%-61.11% across combinations.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The decision log (a persistent typed JSON file consulted before every new task, section 3.3) measurably beat the more generic to-do-list and session-summary strategies for continuity -- a concrete measured instance of MF's docs-as-truth stance winning over generic session narration.

The to-do-list strategy (agent-context/todo/*.json tracking step/status/notes, Figure 3.11) is a direct instance of MF's PLAN-ESTADO anchor -- plan state as first-class persistent memory -- though the thesis measured it as LESS effective than the decision log for continuity (section 5.3).

Measured token/time/cost across all 5 combinations (Figures 4.7-4.9) shows that persisting MORE context (combination 5, all 3 strategies) increased cost AND degraded quality via 'context rot' (section 5.3), confirming MF's stance that context growth has a point of diminishing or negative returns.

notes: Ancla: section 3.3.1 (5 combinations definition) + section 5.2-5.3 discussion (decision log = combination 3 best) + Figures 4.7-4.9. This is a Bachelor's/Master's thesis (Lund Univ. + Bosch R&D), small-N (3 iterations/combination, single mock project) -- weaker evidence strength than peer-reviewed venues, but directly on-topic for MF's context-management/continuity question.

cita: Shekar et al. (2026). GitOfThoughts: Version-Controlled Reasoning and Agent Memory You Can Replay, Diff, and Merge.
problema: LLM agent reasoning (chain-of-thought steps, pruned search branches, reflection/self-criticism buffers) leaves no durable trace once an episode ends -- it cannot be replayed, diffed, or merged across agents, or independently audited -- unlike code and infrastructure, which are version-controlled by default; this blocks reproducibility, incident review, and cross-agent memory transfer.
mecanismo: GitOfThoughts stores an agent's reasoning tree as an actual git repository: each scored thought is a commit (author/timestamp/content-hash), scores become git notes, validation outcomes become tags (success_*/failed_*), exploration paths are branches, and retrieval is stock git primitives (log --grep, -S pickaxe, tag filters, ranked by a confidence-weighted score). A pluggable MemoryBackend interface lets the same agent swap between five substrates (none/markdown/vector/graph/git) with a one-line change, isolating substrate choice from agent logic; cross-agent memory merge is a literal git fetch+merge, surfacing contradictory lessons as merge conflicts instead of silently concatenating them.
evaluacion: Pre-registered controlled evaluation across two benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500) plus a ScienceWorld arm, two backbones (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct), two transfer regimes (cross-problem, cross-episode), and up to n=500, comparing five memory substrates against a no-memory control and against test-time-scaling arms (self-consistency, static few-shot, verifier best-of-N); includes a dedicated cosine-similarity sweep between test problem and memory case, and a fairness/reproducibility audit performed via git's own primitives (Table 2).
numeros_clave: No memory substrate reliably improves accuracy on novel problems across 2 benchmarks, 2 backbones, up to n=500 (all confidence intervals cross zero); a promising +15pp git trend at n=40 (GPQA) collapsed to +1.0pp [-10.2,+11.2] on pre-registered n=98 replication. Memory only helps above a 'copyability threshold' cosine~0.8: near-duplicate/paraphrase retrieval gives +12 to +13.5pp (7B) and +22.5 to +28.5pp (32B, scale steepens this), while same-method-different-numbers (cosine 0.72, non-copyable) is null (-4.1pp [-9.7,+1.5], replicates at 32B: -3.6pp). Self-consistency (5x) is the only arm that reliably beats no-memory on novel problems: +3.4pp [+0.6,+6.2] at n=500. Per-write/read cost (Table 3): git ~15.4ms write / ~48.0ms read vs vector 30.4ms/20.3ms -- git pays a small absolute cost for full auditability. System headline (47.0% vs 33.0% baseline on GPQA) is explicitly attributed to MCQ-aware expansion plus a much larger compute budget, NOT git or memory (Table 8, an admitted confound).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Git-native storage of reasoning as commits/notes/tags gives replay, line-level diff, and signed provenance (section 3.4) -- a maximal-strength confirmation of MF's docs-as-verifiable-truth stance, extended to REASONING traces, not just decisions.

The paper's central, pre-registered, replicated finding is itself negative knowledge -- cross-problem memory reliably does NOT improve novel-problem accuracy below the cosine~0.8 copyability threshold (Table 4-7) -- directly confirming MF's NEGATIVO anchor: a well-evidenced null result prevents costly re-derivation of a false hypothesis.

The paper's core methodological stance -- measure retrieval empirically with pre-registered escalating-N replications rather than assume a memory design helps -- is a strong confirmation of MF's G-M2 anchor; it also empirically bounds where retrieval helps (recurring/near-duplicate workloads only).

Git-native cross-agent memory merge surfaces contradictory lessons as CONFLICTS instead of silently concatenating them (section 3.1, 'injected contradictory lessons surfaced as merge conflicts that simple concatenation silently retained') -- a concrete provenance/conflict-detection mechanism MF could adopt.

notes: Ancla: Table 4-7 (main null result + copyability-threshold sweep), Table 8 (system headline confound explicitly stated), section 3.1 (merge-conflict surfacing demo). Rigorous pre-registered methodology (falsifiable hypotheses, replication after a promising n=40 trend, a retracted early result) -- high-value paper for MF.

cita: Slednev (2026). Deterministic Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents: Hybrid Retrieval, Document Graph, and Write-Path Scalability in Air-Gapped Environments.
problema: Existing LLM-agent memory systems (MemGPT, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti) push generative LLM calls into the WRITE path (fact/entity extraction, coreference resolution, contradiction reconciliation), which is economically costly (indexing cost scales with LLM calls, restricting deployment to small local models in air-gapped settings) and epistemologically risky (a generatively-populated store can contain claims with no correspondence to the input, with untraceable provenance).
mecanismo: Persistent memory is built with NO generative LLM calls in the write path: the source of truth is version-controlled Markdown documents (a git repository per knowledge space); a derived index is built by fully deterministic algorithms -- full-text search with Russian morphology, dense vector embeddings (bge-m3), and a document graph combining explicit author-written wiki-links with automatically detected morphology-robust 'unlinked mentions' (ghost edges). Query-time retrieval fuses lexical and dense pools via Reciprocal Rank Fusion; new/changed documents get a 'pending review' status and only human-confirmed documents reach generative consumers (trust quarantine). All generative work is deferred entirely to the reader agent.
evaluacion: Two hand-verified corpora (T1: 29 docs/100 questions; T2: 68 docs/50 questions) comparing hybrid retrieval modes (naive/iterative full-text search, semantic seeds, graph expansion, fusion) against a manually-checked reference and against Graphiti (an LLM-extraction baseline), measured via hit@5, MRR, and multi-hop recall; plus a write-path scalability study on an open corpus of 3,600 Russian Wikipedia articles at 5 ingestion scales (250-3600 docs), profiled with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to localize a superlinear-degradation root cause before and after an SQL-side fix.
numeros_clave: Hybrid fusion protocol reaches hit@5 88-89% and multi-hop recall 93-100% on both corpora; graph expansion raises multi-hop recall from 27-33% to 73-80%. Graphiti (LLM-extraction baseline, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Q4_K_M) reaches only 42% (67% at fact level) at ~700x the indexing time (68 docs: ~10s deterministic vs 2h04min for Graphiti, ~500 generative-LLM calls). On the 3,600-document scalability corpus, the unoptimized write path degraded superlinearly (median single write 166ms to 846ms, 5.1x, as ghost edges accumulate); after localizing 3 O(N) queries via EXPLAIN ANALYZE and moving normalization into indexed SQL, write time degraded only 1.4x (107 to 147ms) with a measured 3.7x ingestion speedup at 3,600 documents, preserving identical graph-edge semantics.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The design's core invariant -- version-controlled, byte-stored Markdown as the sole source of truth, with the derived index fully rebuildable via deterministic re-indexing (section 2.1) -- is a strong external confirmation of MF's Tier-1 docs-as-truth / derived-index-as-cache stance.

Removing generative LLM calls from the write path cuts indexing cost ~700x vs an LLM-extraction baseline (section 3.2, ~10s vs 2h04min for 68 docs) -- directly confirms MF's cost-economy priority: keep expensive judgment out of high-volume paths.

The paper explicitly names the epistemological risk of generative write paths (fabricated entities/facts observed in the Graphiti baseline run, section 3.2) and mitigates it with a human-confirmation quarantine before any document reaches generative consumers (section 2.1) -- confirms MF's provenance/anti-drift FIDELIDAD anchor.

The paper explicitly measures lexical-vs-semantic complementarity by question category (section 3.1: lexical wins on exact terms MRR 0.66 vs 0.53, semantic wins on paraphrases 0.57 vs 0.37) rather than assuming one retrieval mode dominates -- a clean instance of MF's measured-retrieval-layer stance.

notes: Ancla: Table 1 (hit@5/multi-hop by mode) + section 3.2 (indexing cost table) + section 3.3 (write-path scalability, Table 2, Figure 6) + section 3.4 (Threats to Validity, explicitly single-author/single-run baseline). Industry preprint (not peer-reviewed), single author employed by the company that built the system (disclosed conflict of interest in the paper itself) -- treat evidence strength accordingly; topic fit is clear, no RECONSIDERAR needed.

cita: Liu et al. (2026). Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today's and Future AI Agent Systems.
problema: Production coding agents (Claude Code) must resolve recurring architectural questions -- where reasoning lives, how context is managed under a bounded window, how memory stays transparent and auditable rather than opaque, and how work is safely delegated across subagents -- but Anthropic publishes user-facing docs, not detailed architectural rationale, so this gap is closed via source-level reverse-engineering of the actual TypeScript codebase rather than marketing description.
mecanismo: From source-level analysis: a four-level CLAUDE.md instruction hierarchy (managed/user/project/local) is loaded as plain Markdown delivered as USER context (not system prompt), so compliance is probabilistic and backed by a separate deterministic permission-rule layer; memory retrieval uses an LLM-based scan of file headers to select up to 5 relevant files rather than embeddings or a vector index (an explicit tradeoff of file-level transparency/editability over entry-level selectivity); a graduated 5-layer compaction pipeline (budget reduction, snip, microcompact, context collapse, auto-compact-summary) applies increasingly aggressive, append-only context reduction only once cheaper layers prove insufficient; and an isolated-subagent delegation architecture (the Agent tool) spawns subagents in separate context windows with restricted tool sets and git-worktree-based isolation, returning only a SUMMARY to the parent (not the full transcript) to bound the cost of delegation.
evaluacion: Qualitative source-code analysis (not a benchmarked accuracy study) of the public Claude Code TypeScript codebase, cross-referenced against Anthropic's official documentation, an internal 132-engineer survey, and longitudinal usage telemetry; contrasted along six design dimensions against two independent open-source agent systems (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent) to show how the same recurring design questions receive different answers under different deployment contexts.
numeros_clave: Community analysis estimates only ~1.6% of Claude Code's codebase is AI decision logic vs 98.4% operational infrastructure. Anthropic's internal survey (132 engineers): ~27% of Claude-Code-assisted tasks were work that would not have been attempted without the tool; users approve 93% of permission prompts. Longitudinal telemetry: auto-approve rate rises from ~20% at fewer than 50 sessions to over 40% by 750 sessions. An independent study cited finds AI-assisted-condition developers scored 17% lower on codebase-comprehension tests (the 'paradox of supervision'). Memory-retrieval design: up to 5 files surfaced per LLM-based header scan; no embeddings or vector index used for CLAUDE.md memory retrieval.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Claude Code deliberately rejects embeddings/vector-index memory retrieval in favor of plain-Markdown, version-controllable CLAUDE.md files scanned by header (section 7.2) -- the exact architecture MF's own CLAUDE.md/docs-as-truth stance already follows, a strong confirmation from the tool MF itself runs on.

The built-in 'Plan' subagent type produces a structured plan as a first-class artifact before execution proceeds (section 8.1) -- a concrete plan-state-as-memory pattern MF's PLAN-ESTADO anchor could formalize further.

The graduated 5-layer compaction pipeline that escalates from cheap (budget reduction) to costly (full model-generated summary) only as needed (section 7.3), plus subagents returning summary-only results to bound delegation cost (section 8.1), directly confirms MF's context-economy priority.

CLAUDE.md content is delivered as probabilistic user-context guidance while a SEPARATE deterministic permission-rule layer enforces safety (section 7.2) -- the same guidance-vs-enforcement split MF's own gate architecture relies on, an explicit design confirmation from Claude Code's own source.

notes: Ancla: Section 7 (CLAUDE.md hierarchy + compaction pipeline, Figures 3/6/7) + Section 8 (subagent delegation) + Section 10 (OpenClaw/Hermes memory-architecture contrast table). Directly and unusually relevant to MF: this paper reverse-engineers the exact tool (Claude Code) MF's own harness runs on.

cita: Tran et al. (2026). MEMRES: A Memory-Augmented Resolver with Confidence Cascade for Agentic Python Dependency Resolution.
problema: Python dependency resolution for legacy/broken code snippets is costly with pure-LLM approaches (the PLLM baseline calls an LLM for every snippet, wasting 60-120s per snippet) even though most failures (Python 2/3 mismatches, known import-name mismatches, version incompatibilities) have deterministic root causes that a model call cannot address any better than a lookup table.
mecanismo: MemRes is a 6-level confidence cascade consulted in strict order before ever calling an LLM: (1) intra-session memory (reuse solutions proven earlier in the same batch for near-duplicate snippets, matched by import-set Jaccard similarity >=0.5), (2) a static compatibility map, (3) ecosystem templates, (4) co-occurrence mining from 50K pre-2020 requirements.txt files, (5) heuristic rules (200+ curated import-to-package mappings, a Python-2 detector, a system-dependency injector), and only then (6) LLM selection as last resort. A self-evolving memory records validated 'tips and shortcuts' at runtime -- new shortcuts are sandbox-validated via a real Docker build before being written -- plus per-package failure anti-patterns; memory is fully reset between independent evaluation runs to prevent cross-run overfitting.
evaluacion: Evaluated on HG2.9K (2,890 Python GitHub Gist snippets with dependency conflicts) using Gemma-2 9B, compared against the PLLM baseline (reported 54.7% success) under an identical benchmark and thresholding; 10 independent randomized-order runs report mean +/- std; an ablation disabling intra-session memory (Level 1) isolates its individual contribution; efficiency metrics (LLM calls per snippet, resolution time, token usage) are measured against PLLM.
numeros_clave: MemRes resolves 2503/2890 (86.6% +/-0.3%, 10-run avg, std +/-9.3 snippets) vs PLLM's 1583/2891 (54.7%) -- recovers 950+ of PLLM's total (conf=0) failures. Ablation (Table 2): disabling intra-session memory (Level 1) drops success from 86.6% to 81.6% (-5.0pp, -146 snippets). Efficiency (Table 3): 68.0% of passing cases resolved with ZERO LLM calls (0.34 LLM calls/snippet avg vs PLLM's 1-5), ~75% token-usage reduction, median resolution 15.2s vs PLLM's ~120-180s. 53.9% of successful resolutions trigger system-level (apt-get) dependency injection. Root-cause breakdown of remaining ~387 failures: ~50% build/C-extension, ~33% unresolvable ImportErrors, ~15% timeouts, ~2% platform-specific.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The confidence cascade calls the LLM ONLY as a last resort after 5 deterministic levels fail (section 2.2), reducing LLM calls by over 60% while improving accuracy (Table 3) -- a strong external confirmation of MF's own 'delegate to gates first, expensive judgment only when no gate resolves it' principle applied to a different domain.

The self-evolving memory records per-package failure statistics as explicit anti-patterns to avoid (section 2.3), a concrete negative-knowledge mechanism MF's NEGATIVO anchor could adopt for its own recipe/gotcha memory.

New shortcuts are validated with a real sandboxed Docker build before being written to memory, and memory is fully reset between independent runs to prevent cross-run leakage/overfitting (section 2.3, section 3.1) -- confirms MF's stance that write-time validation and reset discipline matter for anti-drift.

A dedicated ablation (Table 2) isolates the exact accuracy contribution of intra-session memory alone (+5.0pp) -- a clean measured-retrieval-value study, confirming MF's stance that a memory component's value must be measured per-component, not assumed.

notes: Ancla: Table 1 (main result) + Table 2 (Level-1 ablation) + Table 3 (efficiency) + section 2.3 (sandboxed shortcut validation) + section 3.1 (leakage/threats-to-validity discipline). Preprint (FSE Companion '26), narrow domain (Python dependency resolution), but the cascade-before-LLM pattern and rigorous leakage auditing transfer directly to MF's cost/gate design.

cita: Zhang & Sun (2026). Knowledge-Based Pull Requests: A Trusted Workflow for Agent-Mediated Knowledge Collaboration.
problema: When AI coding agents let external collaborators generate large, plausible patches quickly, the receiving project's bottleneck shifts from code production to collaboration burden: judging fit, provenance, and long-term responsibility from a final diff that is a lossy record of the local exploration that produced it, since traditional PRs treat external code as the default merge candidate and expose only the final diff, not the rationale, evidence, or rejected alternatives behind it.
mecanismo: Knowledge-Based Pull Requests (KPR) is a 7-stage trusted workflow that separates 'should this knowledge enter the project?' from 'is this code an acceptable implementation?': an external collaborator's local code/tests/cleaned agent trace are distilled by an extraction agent into a structured, human-confirmed knowledge package with provenance (never raw trace, never external code as the merge candidate); a transformation agent renders it into reviewer-preferred forms (design memo, risk checklist, test plan); project-side reviewers gate the KNOWLEDGE first; only if accepted does a project-owned INNER TRUSTED coding agent regenerate candidate code from the package inside the receiving project's own repository context, conventions, and security policy (external code is only an evidence source, never itself the merge candidate); ordinary code review/CI/merge follows on the project-generated code.
evaluacion: Primarily a conceptual workflow/architecture paper with an explicit cost-accounting model (Table 1), plus a minimal controlled simulation pilot over 7 merged public PRs (<=5 files, <=350 changed lines) scoring artifacts under 5 conditions (normal-summary baseline, full KPR package, description ablation, diff ablation, synthetic poisoned-patch) against 3 author-scored dimensions (intent, evidence, implementation sufficiency); explicitly framed as exercising the artifact/scoring protocol, not estimating population-level effects -- no maintainer study yet.
numeros_clave: Table 3 (7-PR pilot, artifacts scored present/total): intent preserved 7/7 in ALL 5 conditions (even the sparse normal-summary baseline). Evidence traceability: normal summary 0/7 vs full KPR package 7/7 vs description-ablation KPR 7/7 vs diff-ablation KPR 0/7 vs poisoned KPR 7/7 -- evidence structuring is the differentiator vs a plain summary, and depends on retaining the diff. Implementation sufficiency: normal summary 0/7, KPR package 6/7, description-ablation 6/7, diff-ablation only 5/7 (weaker without patch content). All 7/7 synthetic-poisoned-patch packages were correctly rejected by the harness as non-legitimate external code (a narrow, harness-level result, not a real adversarial-robustness claim).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: KPR's core mechanism -- external code is only an evidence SOURCE, and the project's own inner trusted agent REGENERATES the mergeable artifact from a confirmed knowledge package (section 3, Figure 1) -- is a strong single-source-of-truth pattern: untrusted input never becomes truth directly, it is re-derived through the project's own authoritative path, directly extending MF's COSTURAS anchor.

The knowledge package explicitly separates claims/evidence/provenance/safety-notes and requires human confirmation before any code regeneration (section 4.1, Table 1) -- confirms MF's provenance/anti-drift stance that an artifact's trustworthiness needs explicit, auditable provenance, not implicit trust in the source.

The project-side 'knowledge review' gate (stage 5, section 4) is a concrete discretionary write-trigger deciding whether external knowledge is admitted into project truth before any code is generated from it -- a direct instance of MF's G-M1 anchor applied to cross-trust-boundary collaboration.

The paper's own cost-accounting model (Table 1) explicitly frames KPR's value as CONDITIONAL -- useful only when agent-handled work is cheaper than reverse-engineering rework -- and admits the pilot does not measure maintainer burden, a useful caution against assuming a new governance layer pays for itself without measurement.

notes: Ancla: Table 1 (cost-accounting model) + Table 3 (7-PR pilot scoring) + section 7 (pilot corpus/conditions) + section 8.2 (proposed factorial follow-up design). Explicitly a conceptual/pilot paper -- author states the pilot 'is not an end-to-end validation' and 'does not validate maintainer burden reduction'; treat evidence strength accordingly.
